_comment: The 19:00 evening queue — the TEDx strand, separate from the 17:00 game clips.
Read by .github/workflows/publish-evening.yml, which copies this over queue.json
inside the runner before calling publish.mjs. The copy is never committed; only
posted.json is. publish.mjs itself is untouched and the 17:00 run is unaffected.
Both runs share posted.json, which is what stops a clip going out twice.
LENGTH MATTERS HERE. Meta's publishing API caps Reels at 90 seconds: Facebook
rejects anything longer outright, and Instagram accepts it but publishes it as an
ordinary video rather than a Reel, which costs most of the reach. The TEDx cuts
running on TikTok include a 1:32 and a 1:37 and would fail on both counts. These
three are the shorter cuts — 32s, 38s, 40s — and are safely inside the limit.
22 Sept: started with the vote clip deliberately. It is the same material that
took 8 views on TikTok against 703 for that day's game clip, despite holding a
9.57s average watch — the highest the account has recorded. Running it on Meta is
the cleanest way to tell whether that was TikTok suppressing third-party footage
or something about the clip itself.

30 Sept: optional per-post "firstComment" — publish.mjs posts it as the account's first comment right after publishing (Max, 30 Sept). FYN 1-4 replaced in place by cold-open cuts; stories 15/13/9 by first-second hook cuts.

Right before a puzzle test: A, Mozart — or B, a Stephen King story? Which gets you the higher score? Both, equally. Against a story instead of silence, the Mozart advantage disappeared — people mostly did better after whichever one they preferred (Nantais & Schellenberg, 1999, Psychological Science). Comment A or B. No changing it now. Find out how you learn → link in bio.

#mozarteffect #studytok #learning #psychology #focus #brainteaser

posts.caption: Close your eyes and picture an apple. How clear is it, from 1 (nothing at all) to 5 (like real life)? About 1 person in 100 sees nothing at all — it's called aphantasia, named in 2015. At the other end, about 3 in 100 see it like real life (Zeman et al., 2020, Cortex). Comment your number. 1s and 5s especially. Find out how you learn → link in bio. #aphantasia #psychology #brainteaser #memory #learning #studytok

Where does a bike's chain go? A, B, C or D? It's C: pedals to the back wheel. In one study, about half of people who rarely ride got a basic part of a bicycle wrong, most often the chain, and nearly all of them had learned to ride one (Lawson, 2006, Memory & Cognition). Comment your letter. No googling. Find out how you learn → link in bio. #bicycle #psychology #brainteaser #memory #learning #studytok

posts.caption: Name the red letter. Was there an X after it? There was — three tenths of a second later. Spot one target and a second one arriving about 0.2–0.45 s later is often missed: the attentional blink (Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell, 1992). Comment X or no X. Be honest. Find out how you learn → link in bio. #attention #attentionalblink #psychology #brainteaser #learning #studytok

posts.caption: How many dots? Don't count. 3 and 4 are instant. 7 isn't: you have to guess. Up to about four, people just see how many. It's called subitizing (Revkin et al., 2008, Psychological Science). Comment your number for the last one. Find out how you learn → link in bio. #subitizing #psychology #brainteaser #workingmemory #learning #studytok

posts.caption: Remember the colours. Four squares: easy. Eight: did one change? One did. Visual memory holds about four things at once — and in the original study, making each one more detailed (colour and angle) didn't lower that, suggesting it counts objects more than details (Luck & Vogel, 1997, Nature). Comment same or changed. No scrolling back. Find out how you learn → link in bio. #workingmemory #memory #psychology #brainteaser #learning #studytok

posts.caption: Remember these words. How many can you keep? Most people keep the last few and the first few, and lose more from the middle: the serial position effect (Murdock, 1962). Straight after a list, the middle is the bit most likely to slip. Comment how many you got. And which.
